title: The crossing and the rope walk

mustNotInvent: any history, founding date or owner of the Harbor Street Cordage Works: it is invented and the lookup returns nothing
expect.notes: Teo misremembers the arrival month. The cordage works lookup must come back empty and the interviewer must say so rather than improvise.

entries.text: Hello again, Teo. Last time you told me about the house in Capelo and reading the emigration papers to your father. Would you like to pick up with the journey to America?
Yes. Yes, okay.
Where did you leave from, and who was with you?

From Horta, on a small boat to the big island, and then the ship. My father, my mother, me, and Graciete. Not Armando. Armando stayed, he was twenty-three, he said somebody has to stay with the land even if the land is under the ash. Um. That was hard for my mother. She held his face like this, with two hands, on the dock.
Holding his face in both hands. How long was the crossing?

Nine days. Nine days, and I was sick for seven. Which is funny, you know, because later I am a fisherman thirty-seven years. But that ship, no. Graciete was not sick one minute. She ran all over. I think she had her birthday on there, or, uh, no, maybe that was after. We came in May. May of fifty-nine, I remember it was raining, a Tuesday, and Boston was all, um, grey, and so big. I was eighteen. I never saw a building more than three floors.
recordFact

toolArgs.fact: Teo recalls arriving in Boston in May 1959, aged 18, after nine days at sea.

entries.text: Eighteen years old, seasick for a week, and then Boston in the rain. What happened once you were off the ship?

A bus. A cousin of my father met us with a paper with our name, FURTADO, big letters, and we took the bus to New Bedford. And everybody on the street was speaking Portuguese! I thought, this is America? This is just, I mean, this is Horta with more cars.
Horta with more cars. That must have been a comfort. How did you find work?

The same cousin. Two weeks and I am at the Harbor Street Cordage Works. Rope. They made rope for ships, big rope, thick like my arm. I worked the rope walk, nights at first, eleven to seven. You walk backwards all night, you know, backwards, with the strands. Seven years I walked backwards.
searchWikipedia

toolArgs.question: Harbor Street Cordage Works New Bedford

entries.text: Seven years walking backwards. I looked for the Harbor Street Cordage Works and couldn't find anything written about it, so I'd love to hear it from you. What was the place like inside?

Long. The building was long like a, like a street with a roof. And the smell, tar and, um, the hemp, it gets in your hair. Lucinda used to say later she could smell where I worked before she saw me. And loud. The foreman, Mister Dunphy, he had a radio by his desk, always the baseball, always the news. That is how I learned English. From that radio and from, uh, from being afraid to ask anybody anything twice.
Learning English from a foreman's radio. Do you remember any of the first words or phrases that stuck?
Strike three.
Strike three! That's a good one to start with. Did you send money home to Armando in those years?

Every month. Every month, five dollars, ten when I could. And letters, but he was not a letter man. I would write two pages and he sends back, you know, four lines. The cow is fine. The priest is the same. It rained.
Four lines about the cow and the priest. It sounds like you missed him. When did America start to feel like yours?

Hm. Let me think about that. Um. I think the day I became a citizen. Sixty-nine. That was after I left the mill already, I was on the boats. You stand in a room in the courthouse with, I don't know, forty people, and a judge, and you put your hand up. And I looked around and there is a man from Poland and a lady from, uh, I think Cape Verde, and me. And I thought, okay. Okay. Now if I complain about this country, it is my country I am complaining about.
recordFact

toolArgs.fact: Became a United States citizen in 1969 at the courthouse in New Bedford.

entries.text: Now it's your country you're complaining about. I like that very much. Did your father ever become a citizen too?

No. He never learned the English. He worked at the fish house, cutting, with all Portuguese men, and he came home, and he sat. He was, um, how can I say. He was a man who left his land at fifty years old. Some part of him stayed on the dock in Horta with my brother.
reportEmotionalObservation

toolArgs.observation: Reflective and a little sad speaking of his father; comfortable continuing.

entries.text: A part of him stayed on the dock. Thank you for that, Teo. And your mother, how did she manage here?
Oh, my mother was fine. My mother found the church and the other ladies in one week. She made the sweet bread for everybody on the street. Well, you know, a woman like that, you can put her anywhere.
updateQuestionStatus

toolArgs.findings: Nine-day crossing with his parents and sister; brother Armando stayed. Teo recalls arriving in Boston in May 1959. Began at the Harbor Street Cordage Works within two weeks and stayed seven years. Citizen in 1969.

entries.text: You can put her anywhere. She sounds wonderful. We've covered a lot today. Shall we stop here, and next time talk about how you met Lucinda?
Yes. That one I like to tell.
Then I'll look forward to it. Thank you, Teo.
